messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] predict detection probability
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] predict detection probability
messages.body_plain:
Nelli

I'm guessing from the name of your model object you have no covariates in your detection function and are probably also using single- rather than double-platform.  I am further guessing you are simply interested in the shape of your detection function--or values of g(x) at particular distances.

Unfortunately, predict() does not give you that.  Documentation for the function says:

"The predicted detection probability is the average probability which is simply the integral divided by the distance range"

You might accomplish what you seek, by using the function detfct() in mrds.  Here is a toy example with the object "bob" being the vector of predicted detection probabilities.

library(Distance)
data(book.tee.data)
tee.data<-book.tee.data$book.tee.dataframe[book.tee.data$book.tee.dataframe$observer==1,]
ds.model <- ds(tee.data,4)
bob <- detfct(distance=seq(0,4,0.01),
              ds.model$ddf$ds$aux$ddfobj)
plot(seq(0,4,.01), bob, type='l')

I am also curious why you want to calculate a detection probability at distance 40km from the trackline.  I would think curvature of the earth would make detection probability vanishingly small at such distances.

Can anyone tell me what I am doing wrong?

Do I need to set the data up differently?

e.g.,
Point 1  Distance 25m   0 birds detected
Point 2  Distance 25m   1 bird detected
Point 2  Distance 50 m  1 birds detected
Point 2  Distance 50 m  1 birds detected

Hey everyone,
I'm hoping there is an easy fix to my problem, I thought I was almost done with my analysis!
I am trying to get monthly abundance estimates for right whales, so I have the month as my Region.label.  We have 16 tracklines (my Sample.Label) that we repeat every survey.  So, trackline 1 gets flown multiple times every month.  Because of this, I summed the effort for trackline 1 for April and this is what I put in the effort column for every sighting that was seen on trackline 1 in April (which now I'm realizing might be my problem?).  When I look at the results,  k = 16 which I think is correct since they are the same tracklines every time.  But, the effort seems to be a problem.  In April, for example, the results list the effort as the sum of the entire effort column from my flatfile.  In the minke data you provide as an example, it somehow knows to pull out the effort for trackline 1 only once for each region (instead of all the times it is listed for each sighting).  Unfortunately, I need the effort for trackline 1 more than once for each region, since we covered it more than once.  Is this possible?

Thank you!
~Laura Ganley

messages.body_plain:
Dear group,

I'm fitting DSMs to point survey data using 'dsm' in R and have become curious about how this model works when the response is changed to 'presence.' Specifically, the response variable is 0 when birds are not detected and 1 when at least 1 individual is detected. In this sense, the data are being treated as presence/absence, but I cannot work out how this model makes adjustments for detection probability. I'm also unable to find literature describing this particular version of the DSM beyond what is listed in the R package vignette.

As an example, my model call is the following, assuming a distance-detection function has already been fit using a hazard rate function:

dsm.pres.1 = dsm( presence ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + s(time), ddf.obj = hr.model, segment.data = seg.data, observation.data=obs.data, weights=1, group=TRUE, family=binomial())

I can reclassify the presence/absence response into 0s & 1s and fit those using gam with family=binomial. However, I get much different coefficient estimates for the effects of x1, x2, x3, and s(time). What is dsm doing here that gam is not doing? More specifically, I notice that even though I have set weights=1, there is an attribute of the fitted model object called 'weights' and also 'working.weights' which are the same vector of weights, distributed between 0 and 0.25 and same length as my data. I can access these via 'dsm.pres.1$weights.'

So my questions are, A) what are these weights and how are they being generated, and B) are they responsible for the difference between the dsm and gam being fit to the same binary response variable with same predictors?

Thanks for considering my question.
best,
Shawn

Hi Shawn, hi listfolks,

The presence response was added for convenience to look at issues with
problem datasets (some years ago!) so data could be formatted easily. It
was not intended for any serious modelling. Detectability is ignored.
This was not obvious in the documentation and wrong in some cases in the
code, so I've made some changes and pushed these to the github version
of the package. I still don't recommend using this option though, better
to use a package that's actually set up for this kind of modelling.

Regarding weights, note that the $weights in the returned object are the
iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) weights from the gam fitting
procedure NOT the "prior" weights given to gam() or dsm(). See
?gamObject/?gam.

Hope this helps,
--dave

messages.body_plain:
Hi Piotr, list,

As I see it, there's no point in simulating distances to then fit detection functions to them. I assume you have no covariates besides distance (things can get messier otherwise!).

It seems easier to just assume that those distances miss at random with respect to distance value and then use only those those observations for which you do have distances for to fit the detection function. Then, assume that the same detection function applies to all observations (with and without distances) and use all the observations for the encounter rate.

I am not sure what is the best way in Distance to define this procedure, but I seem to recall that there's a way you can use detection functions fit to a subset of data to provide detectability information for all the data. Others?

have a good weekend!

Cheers,

T

messages.body_plain:
Hello all.

I'm here in behalf of a little team of french birders from the Auvergne LPO who've been using Distance 6.2
for around 3 years now for at least 3 multi-species studies
(if you read french, see https://distancesampling.blogspot.fr/p/un-collectif-dornithologues.html).

We have been using the MCDS engine for estimating the populations of birds of around 25 species,
with some tens of line transects and around 300 points transects, so it's quite a lot of work,
achieved til now with the great Distance 6.2 sofware.

Now, after using the limited (AFAWK) automation features of Distance, we are willing to go
one step further and run our analyses more automatically, at least to do a first auto-sorting
of the "best" models and "best" truncation distances (left and right side)

(very roughly said, something like auto-running analyses for "all" combinations of models and left/right
 truncation values, and then sort-out the "best" analyses from some criteria like AIC, Chi2, KSp ... etc)

We know that this is possible through programming with the R language / infrastructure,
thanks to Distance-specific R modules, and this is great !

But we'd like to know :
* if some of you have already achieved this kind of programming work,
* if so, if you'd be ready to share your code,
* if some of you have already worked on the same target, but using Python
  (there's no Distance interface to this language, but it's quite straightforward to code,
   as it's only about running MCDS.exe and reading/writing Distance output/input files)

Thanks in advance fro your help.

Jean-Philippe.

messages.subject: MCDS : What's the right way of dealing with "no observation" data ?
messages.subject_clean: MCDS : What's the right way of dealing with "no observation" data ?
messages.body_plain:
Hello all.

Again from Auvergne (Southern center of France), where we are using distance sampling
to estimate common birds populations on some sites ...

When preparing field collected data in order to import it into Distance, for each bird species, and for each transect,
we add data lines with no distance in order to take the absence of observation of the species into account.

Now, after 2 years of field collection, we have a data set where each point transect has been surveyed twice.

We tried 2 alternatives about "no observation" data lines (for each point transect and each species) :
1) 1 "no observation" line per survey where the species has not been contacted ;
     that is at most 2 lines here, 1 for 2016 and 1 for 2017, if the species has never been contacted on the point transect during the 2 years
     or only 1 if the species has been contacted only 1 year  on the point
     or 0 if  the species has been contacted each year
2) only 1 "no observation" line where the species has never been contacted on the point transect during the 2 years,
     or 0 "no observation" line if the species has been contacted at least once during the 2 years on this point.

And these 2 methods give quite different density results (of course, we are comparing the same observation input data and the same model and adjustment function).

Do you have an idea about which method we should use here ?

Thanks in advance.
